courses.title: Voltage, current and complete circuits
courses.summary: Trace energy and charge through a sensor node before connecting its first wire.

lessons.title: A circuit needs a return path
lessons.text: A supply transfers energy to a load when charge can circulate through a complete path. An open switch interrupts that path. Conventional current flows from the positive supply through the load toward the negative terminal; electrons in metal drift the other way. A wire bypassing the load creates a short with potentially excessive current.

lessons.title: Voltage is a difference
lessons.text: Voltage measures energy per charge between two points, in volts (V). Current is charge flow per second, in amperes (A). Resistance opposes current, in ohms (Ω). Ground is the chosen 0 V reference, not a place where current disappears. Connected non-isolated modules normally need a common signal reference.

lessons.title: Read values with units
lessons.text: 1 A equals 1,000 mA; 1 mA equals 1,000 µA. A 3.3 V output means 3.3 V relative to its ground. It does not promise any particular load current. Before powering a node, identify the supply, load, signal and return conductors, and check the required supply polarity and voltage.

courses.workedExample: A sensor takes 0.008 A from a 3.3 V supply: its current is 8 mA. A voltmeter between VCC and GND should read about 3.3 V. Disconnecting the return opens the intended circuit; do not assume the data wire is a substitute return. Restore the correct ground connection before evaluating its readings.
courses.application: Draw a sensor node with four labelled connections: supply positive, supply return, sensor supply and sensor data. Trace the complete power loop separately from the information path.

lab.task: Follow the LED current path from the output, through the resistor and LED, back to ground. Use the inspector to compare voltage and current units.

courses.title: Ohm’s law and resistor selection
courses.summary: Calculate current, choose an LED resistor and allow for real component tolerances.

lessons.title: Relate voltage, current and resistance
lessons.text: For an ohmic resistor, V = I × R. Rearrange to I = V / R or R = V / I. Use volts, amperes and ohms in the same calculation. The voltage in this equation is the drop across the resistor itself, not automatically the entire supply.

lessons.title: Size a current-limiting resistor
lessons.text: An LED is nonlinear and needs current limiting. In a simple series circuit, subtract its assumed forward voltage from the supply, then divide by target current. Select a standard resistor at or above the result to avoid exceeding that target under the stated assumptions. Check the GPIO current capability separately.

lessons.title: Design for variation
lessons.text: Resistor tolerance means the actual resistance differs from its label. LED forward voltage and supply voltage also vary. The highest LED current occurs with the highest supply, lowest forward voltage and lowest resistance. Absolute maximum ratings are damage boundaries, not sensible operating targets. Leave margin and verify the actual part datasheet.

courses.workedExample: Assume a 5 V supply, a 2 V LED drop and a 10 mA target. R = (5 − 2) / 0.010 = 300 Ω. Choosing 330 Ω gives about 9.1 mA. The resistor dissipates (3 V)² / 330 Ω ≈ 0.027 W. This is a nominal estimate; the simulated LED and GPIO have additional resistance, so live values can differ.

courses.title: Series, parallel and voltage dividers
courses.summary: Use circuit laws to distribute power and scale sensor voltages.

lessons.title: Series paths and loop voltage
lessons.text: Series components share one current because there is no branch between them. Their resistances add: Rtotal = R1 + R2. Kirchhoff’s voltage law says the signed voltage changes around a closed loop sum to zero. A 5 V source can therefore balance resistor drops of 2 V and 3 V.

lessons.title: Parallel branches and node current
lessons.text: Parallel components share the same two nodes and therefore the same voltage. Branch currents add at the supply. Kirchhoff’s current law says current entering a node equals current leaving it. For two parallel resistors, Req = R1 × R2 / (R1 + R2); it is smaller than either resistor.

lessons.title: A divider is a signal source
lessons.text: With Rtop from input to output and Rbottom from output to ground, an unloaded divider gives Vout = Vin × Rbottom / (Rtop + Rbottom). A connected load is in parallel with Rbottom and changes the ratio. A divider can scale a high-impedance measurement input; it is a poor replacement for a regulated module power supply.

courses.workedExample: A 5 V signal feeds 10 kΩ on top and 20 kΩ below: Vout ≈ 3.33 V without a load. Adding a 20 kΩ load makes the lower equivalent 10 kΩ, so Vout falls to 2.5 V. For a real 3.3 V input, also check input limits and worst-case tolerances; a nominal ratio alone does not establish compatibility.
courses.application: Sketch a battery measurement divider. Label the input range, resistor values, ADC reference and maximum allowed input. Recalculate with the ADC or other load included.

courses.title: Power, energy and battery budgets
courses.summary: Estimate heat and runtime while separating average consumption from current peaks.

lessons.title: Power becomes work and heat
lessons.text: Electrical power is P = V × I, measured in watts. For a resistor, P = I²R = V²/R. Energy is power multiplied by time; watt-hours are convenient for batteries. A resistor’s wattage rating describes heat-handling capability under specified conditions. It does not set the current by itself.

lessons.title: Average current predicts runtime
lessons.text: For states repeating in a cycle, multiply each state current by its fraction of the cycle, then add. Capacity in mAh divided by average mA gives an ideal runtime in hours only when both refer to the same battery-side current. Regulators, temperature, ageing and cutoff reduce usable energy.

lessons.title: Peak current sizes the supply
lessons.text: A radio may sleep most of the time but demand a brief burst during transmission. The supply, regulator and wiring must support that peak without the voltage falling below operating limits. Average current determines energy use; peak current and voltage drop determine whether the node stays running.

courses.workedExample: Assume battery-side current is 80 mA for 10% of each cycle and 1 mA for 90%. Iavg = 80 × 0.1 + 1 × 0.9 = 8.9 mA. A nominal 1,000 mAh battery gives an ideal 112 hours. This estimate excludes capacity loss and does not prove the supply can deliver the 80 mA peak.
courses.application: Make a state table for sensing, processing, transmitting and sleeping. Record duration, battery-side current and the maximum simultaneous load.

lab.task: Compare the LED at low and high duty cycle. Use the average-load concept, but calculate battery runtime separately; this lab does not model a battery discharge curve.

courses.title: Breadboards, schematics and measurement
courses.summary: Turn a schematic into connected nodes and use measurements to find wiring mistakes.

lessons.title: Read connectivity, not drawing distance
lessons.text: A schematic describes electrical connections, not physical placement. A node includes every point joined by an ideal wire. Junction dots distinguish connected crossings from unconnected crossings. Identify component pin names and polarity before translating the drawing into breadboard holes; adjacent-looking holes are not always connected.

lessons.title: Understand the breadboard strips
lessons.text: In VoltQuest, holes a–e in one numbered row form a strip; f–j form another across the centre gap. Power rails are separate from these strips and from each other. Real breadboards can have split rails: inspect markings and test continuity while unpowered. Give each component leg and cable plug its own physical hole.

lessons.title: Measure the right quantity
lessons.text: Measure voltage across two points with the meter in parallel. Measure current by opening the path and inserting a correctly configured, fused meter in series. Never put a meter in current mode directly across a supply. Resistance and continuity tests require an unpowered circuit; discharge capacitors appropriately first. Use low-voltage circuits for these exercises.

courses.workedExample: An LED leg is in a20 and its jumper is in b20, so both share one strip. A jumper in b21 would be a different node. If the LED stays dark, compare measured voltages along the expected path, then remove power and check continuity. Do not diagnose a missing connection by increasing the supply voltage.
courses.application: Annotate a simple schematic with node names, then create a connection checklist. Verify one node at a time before running firmware.

courses.title: Capacitors, RC timing and decoupling
courses.summary: Explain transient behaviour and choose where capacitors belong in an IoT power path.

lessons.title: Store charge, oppose rapid voltage changes
lessons.text: A capacitor stores charge according to Q = C × V. Capacitance is measured in farads, commonly µF and nF. Its current follows I = C × dV/dt, so abrupt voltage changes require current. An ideal capacitor carries no steady DC current after settling, but real parts have leakage, resistance and voltage limits.

lessons.title: Predict an RC response
lessons.text: A resistor charging a capacitor creates a time constant τ = R × C. Starting from zero, the capacitor reaches about 63% of a constant applied voltage after one τ and over 99% after five τ. This is an exponential approach, not a linear ramp. Increasing R or C slows the response.

lessons.title: Decouple near the load
lessons.text: A local decoupling capacitor supplies short current changes while the upstream supply responds. Short connections reduce unwanted inductance. Bulk capacitance supports longer changes, but cannot fix an undersized supply indefinitely. Follow the device and regulator requirements for capacitance and ESR. Respect electrolytic polarity and voltage rating.

courses.workedExample: For 10 kΩ and 10 µF, τ = 10,000 × 0.000010 = 0.1 s. With a 3.3 V step, the capacitor reaches about 2.09 V after 0.1 s and 3.28 V after 0.5 s. These are analytical RC values; the breadboard teaching solver does not reproduce this full transient curve.
courses.application: Draw local decoupling beside a sensor supply pin and a bulk capacitor beside a pulsed load. Explain which current interval each supports and what still determines the supply rating.

lab.task: Observe software debounce in the button lab. Compare it on paper with an RC filter; the lab demonstrates software timing rather than capacitor transients.

formulas.equation: τ = R × C; Vc(t) = Vs × (1 − e^(−t/τ))

courses.title: Diodes, transistors and load drivers
courses.summary: Control a larger load with a small logic signal and manage inductive energy.

lessons.title: Diodes conduct directionally
lessons.text: A diode conducts strongly in its forward direction and blocks reverse current within its limits. Forward voltage is not a universal constant: it depends on device type, current and temperature. Check polarity, current rating and reverse-voltage rating. A diode used for polarity protection introduces a voltage drop and heat.

lessons.title: Separate control from load power
lessons.text: A GPIO is a signal source with limited current. An NPN transistor or suitable logic-level MOSFET can switch a load supplied from a separate power branch. A low-side NPN places its emitter at ground and collector at the load return, with a base resistor. MOSFET selection uses on-resistance at the actual gate voltage, not threshold voltage alone.

lessons.title: Give coil current a turn-off path
lessons.text: Motors and relay coils store magnetic energy. Interrupting their current can create a high voltage. For a simple DC low-side coil driver, a flyback diode is connected across the coil, cathode toward supply positive and anode toward the switched low side. It normally blocks and conducts during turn-off. Choose a driver and diode for the actual load.

courses.workedExample: Suppose a small NPN switch needs 5 mA base drive and has an assumed 0.7 V base-emitter drop. From a 3.3 V GPIO, Rbase = (3.3 − 0.7) / 0.005 = 520 Ω. This only sizes a nominal base resistor; verify saturation, GPIO limits, transistor dissipation and load startup current before selecting real parts.

courses.title: Analog signals, ADCs and PWM
courses.summary: Convert sensor voltage into numbers and control output with timed digital pulses.

lessons.title: Separate analog and digital meaning
lessons.text: An analog signal represents a continuous quantity, such as a potentiometer position encoded as voltage. A digital input classifies voltage into logic states using thresholds. Voltages between valid low and high ranges are not reliable logic values. Neither type of input may exceed its electrical limits.

lessons.title: Quantisation is not accuracy
lessons.text: An N-bit ADC offers 2ᴺ codes. In a simple endpoint-scaled teaching conversion, code ≈ Vin / Vref × (2ᴺ − 1). More bits give finer code spacing, but reference error, noise and calibration still affect accuracy. Actual ESP32 input ranges depend on attenuation and chip configuration; the lab uses a simplified 0–3.3 V model.

lessons.title: PWM changes time, not pulse height
lessons.text: Pulse-width modulation switches an output between low and high. Duty cycle is on-time divided by period. Frequency is cycles per second. An ideal 3.3 V waveform at 25% duty has a time-average of 0.825 V, but the instantaneous high is still 3.3 V. Filtering and load behaviour determine the resulting physical output.

courses.workedExample: For an ideal 10-bit, 5 V endpoint model, 2.5 V maps to about 512 of 0–1023. An 8-bit PWM command of 64 out of 255 gives about 25% duty. These numbers describe separate operations: the ADC measures an input; PWM schedules output pulses. PWM is not a DAC producing a steady quarter-supply voltage.

courses.title: Logic levels, pull-ups and shared buses
courses.summary: Connect digital devices without floating inputs, voltage conflicts or bus contention.

lessons.title: Match electrical levels first
lessons.text: A module supply rating is different from its signal-pin tolerance. A 5 V-powered module may emit a 5 V signal that is unsuitable for a 3.3 V-only input. Check output-high/low and input-high/low specifications, absolute limits and common reference. A level translator must match voltage, direction and signalling type.

lessons.title: Give an input a default state
lessons.text: A high-impedance input can float when nothing drives it. A pull-up resistor weakly connects it to the logic supply. A button to ground then reads high when released and low when pressed. Pull-downs reverse the arrangement. A bias resistor sets an electrical default; software debounce separately handles repeated transitions from a mechanical contact.

lessons.title: Open-drain buses need pull-ups
lessons.text: I2C uses shared SDA and SCL with pull-ups and devices that can pull lines low. Pull-up voltage must suit every connected pin. Smaller resistance improves rise time but increases low-state current; cable and input capacitance limit speed. Push-pull outputs must not fight each other. UART normally connects TX to RX, not TX to TX.

courses.workedExample: With a 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V and a closed button to ground, about 0.33 mA flows through the resistor. Released, the input is high. Two 4.7 kΩ pull-ups fitted by two modules act in parallel as 2.35 kΩ: account for built-in pull-ups when assembling a bus.

lessons.title: Sample information, not just numbers
lessons.text: Choose sampling rate from how quickly the measured quantity can change. Frequencies above half the sampling rate can alias into misleading slower signals. Analog filtering before conversion limits unwanted high-frequency content. Averaging can reduce random noise in sampled data, but does not remove systematic offset or undo aliasing.

lessons.title: Make decisions robust
lessons.text: A single threshold can chatter when readings fluctuate near it. Hysteresis uses separate on and off thresholds and remembers the current state. Validate sensor range and freshness before acting. A disconnected sensor must not silently become a valid zero measurement. Define how the device behaves during stale data, reboot and lost communication.

lessons.title: Review the whole chain
lessons.text: A useful node has a power path, sensing path, processing step and communication path. Review supply peaks, voltage compatibility, component tolerances and fault states together. Test one change at a time, compare against a known input and record expected versus observed values. Simulator success verifies the teaching model; hardware still needs electrical and environmental validation.

courses.workedExample: For a fan controller, turn on above 30 °C and turn off below 28 °C. At 29 °C, retain the previous state. If no valid sample arrives within the chosen timeout, enter a documented fault state instead of continuing to display stale data as current. The timeout and fault action depend on the application.

lessons.title: Microcontroller or Linux computer
lessons.text: Uno and Nano are microcontroller boards that run a firmware loop. ESP32 adds integrated wireless capabilities. Raspberry Pi 4/5 are computers that can run Linux on real hardware. Select from workload, timing, power and connectivity needs. In VoltQuest, Pi runs only the documented restricted GPIO/Python teaching subset; it does not emulate Linux.

lessons.title: Read the pin map for this board
lessons.text: Supply pins, grounds and GPIOs have different jobs. Check input-only pins, analog capability, bus pins and startup restrictions. Uno/Nano use 5 V logic; the ESP32 boards and Pi GPIO use 3.3 V logic. A Pi 5 V header supply pin does not make its GPIO 5 V tolerant. Physical pin numbers and GPIO names are different numbering systems.

lessons.title: Select by interfaces and operating budget
lessons.text: List every required sensor and output before allocating pins. Reserve bus connections and count available ADC channels. Pi 4/5 do not provide general-purpose analog inputs on their header; a real analog sensor needs an external ADC. Confirm the exact ESP32 variant rather than assuming identical ADC, DAC or radio capabilities across the family.

courses.workedExample: A node needs one analog measurement, a status LED and WiFi. An ESP32 is a plausible starting point: reserve a suitable ADC pin and output pin, then check rail current and WiFi/ADC restrictions. A Pi could do the job with added ADC hardware, but its power and software requirements differ. Choose from requirements, not board size alone.

lessons.title: Specify more than the nominal value
lessons.text: A resistor specification includes resistance, tolerance and power rating. A capacitor specification includes capacitance, voltage rating, polarity where applicable and characteristics such as ESR. A BOM should identify a usable part, not just say resistor or capacitor. A physically fitting replacement may still be electrically wrong.

lessons.title: Recognise the circuit role
lessons.text: A series resistor limits current; two resistors can divide voltage; a pull-up defines an undriven input. Decoupling capacitors connect across the local supply and return. These roles are different, even when the parts look alike. A pull-up is not a replacement for an LED series resistor, and a capacitor is not a regulator.

lessons.title: Connections are components too
lessons.text: Real jumpers and connectors have resistance, current limits and mechanical failure modes. Label supply polarity, provide strain relief and avoid sharing one hole between a component leg and a cable. Keep long noisy load returns away from sensitive measurements where practical. Verify continuity and pin order rather than trusting wire colours.

courses.workedExample: A 10 kΩ ±1% pull-up can range from 9.9 to 10.1 kΩ. A 100 nF decoupler is 0.1 µF. In a parts list, add the resistor’s power rating and capacitor’s voltage/type requirements. If the module already contains pull-ups or decoupling, read its schematic before duplicating them.

lessons.title: Single-colour indicators
lessons.text: A discrete LED has an anode and cathode and needs a controlled current path. Forward voltage depends on colour and device construction. Size the series resistor for the selected supply and target current. Reversing polarity normally prevents illumination; excessive reverse voltage can damage the part. Brightness is not a reliable current meter.

lessons.title: RGB means separate channels
lessons.text: A basic RGB LED contains red, green and blue emitters with a shared anode or cathode. Each active colour channel needs its own current control because forward voltages differ. PWM mixes apparent colour and brightness. Identify the common pin and pin order from the exact part rather than assuming every four-leg LED is identical.

lessons.title: Addressable pixels include a controller
lessons.text: Addressable pixels accept timed digital data and contain their own channel drivers. Data direction, supply voltage and logic compatibility matter. Pixel count and brightness determine load demand. Follow the selected product’s guidance for power distribution, local capacitance and data-line conditioning. VoltQuest’s pixel model simplifies current and signal timing; a real strip needs its own power calculation.

courses.workedExample: Assume a selected pixel’s datasheet budget is 45 mA at the intended maximum setting. Twelve pixels then need 12 × 45 = 540 mA, before the controller. This is an exercise assumption, not a universal NeoPixel specification. Reducing brightness may reduce average demand, but the supply and wiring still need a verified worst-case design.

courses.title: Buttons, potentiometers and touch inputs

lessons.title: Buttons need bias and debounce
lessons.text: A momentary button connects contacts only while pressed. A pull-up or pull-down defines its released voltage. Mechanical contacts may bounce through several transitions during one press. Debounce accepts a new state only after suitable stability or timing rules; edge detection then turns a held state into one action.

lessons.title: A potentiometer is an adjustable divider
lessons.text: Connect the two ends of a potentiometer to the permitted supply and ground, and its wiper to an ADC input. The wiper voltage moves between the endpoint voltages. A wiper is not a high-current power output. Check the selected board has an ADC and handle jitter near boundaries in software.

lessons.title: Touch detects capacitance changes
lessons.text: A capacitive touch input detects changes in coupling rather than a metal contact closing. Thresholds depend on pad geometry, enclosure, moisture and baseline conditions. Calibrate and test on the target device. The prepared ESP32 touch lab uses a deterministic touched/untouched teaching input rather than reproducing a real electrode’s environment.

courses.workedExample: A pull-up button reads HIGH when released. To toggle a light once per press, debounce the reading and act only on the accepted HIGH-to-LOW transition. Repeatedly toggling on every loop while LOW makes one held press generate many actions. For a control dial, map the ADC range to a bounded application value.

lessons.title: Choose the measured quantities
lessons.text: DHT22 provides temperature and relative humidity using its own timed digital protocol. BME280 provides temperature, humidity and pressure through I2C or SPI on real hardware; the VoltQuest module uses I2C. BMP280 does not add humidity just because its name is similar. Select from range, accuracy, response time and interface, not only the number of printed digits.

lessons.title: Distinguish chip and breakout board
lessons.text: A bare sensor and a breakout containing a regulator or level translation can have different supply requirements. Verify the exact module schematic and logic levels. I2C devices need the correct address and bus pins; DHT data is not an I2C SDA connection. Physical sensor placement also matters: nearby regulators and sunlight can bias temperature readings.

lessons.title: Publish units and validity
lessons.text: Read at a cadence supported by the selected sensor rather than as fast as the processor can loop. Check read failures, range and sample age. Relative humidity is a percentage; pressure may be reported in Pa or hPa, with 100 Pa = 1 hPa. Preserve units in messages and distinguish stale data from a fresh measurement.

courses.workedExample: A weather node receives 101,300 Pa and 24.5 °C. Publish pressure as 1,013 hPa only after dividing by 100, and keep the temperature unit explicit. If the next read fails, report validity=false with the last sample’s age; do not fabricate a 0 °C reading. A timestamp describes freshness, not sensor accuracy.

courses.summary: Compare what LDR, PIR and ultrasonic parts can actually tell an IoT device.

lessons.title: Light-dependent resistance
lessons.text: An LDR changes resistance with illumination. Place it in a divider to obtain a voltage for an ADC. The voltage direction depends on whether the LDR is above or below the divider midpoint. Its response is nonlinear and part-dependent: an uncalibrated ADC number is not automatically a lux measurement.

lessons.title: Motion is not distance or identity
lessons.text: A PIR detects changes in received infrared radiation across its sensing zones. A module often presents a digital motion output with its own hold time. It does not identify a person or reliably prove that a still room is empty. Warm-up, field of view and the real module’s supply/output levels need checking.

lessons.title: Ultrasonic time of flight
lessons.text: An ultrasonic module sends a sound pulse and reports the round-trip echo time. Distance is speed of sound × time / 2. Temperature, surface angle and absorption affect the result. Use an echo timeout and distinguish no echo from zero distance. Check whether a module’s echo output needs scaling before reaching a 3.3 V GPIO.

courses.workedExample: Assume sound travels at 343 m/s. A 2 ms round trip corresponds to 343 × 0.002 / 2 = 0.343 m, or 34.3 cm. Forgetting the return journey doubles the reported distance. No echo before a timeout means unavailable or out of range, not necessarily an object touching the sensor.

courses.title: Buzzers, servos, motors and relay modules
courses.summary: Turn logic into sound or movement while separating commands from load power.

lessons.title: Match the actuator to the task
lessons.text: An active buzzer contains an oscillator; a passive buzzer needs a changing drive signal to produce a tone. A positional hobby servo interprets control pulses as a target position. A DC motor rotates with behaviour set by its electrical and mechanical load; PWM alone does not provide exact speed feedback.

lessons.title: Supply movement from a rated driver
lessons.text: Servos have separate signal, power and ground connections. Motors need a driver sized for startup and stall current; reverse rotation requires an appropriate bidirectional circuit such as an H-bridge. Shared non-isolated control needs a common reference. A simulation command angle does not certify a real mechanism’s travel, load capacity or endpoint safety.

lessons.title: Relay contacts are separate from the coil
lessons.text: A relay module’s control side energises a coil; its COM, NO and NC contacts switch a separate load path. NO is open and NC is closed to COM when the coil is de-energised. Check control polarity, contact ratings and any onboard driver/protection. Use only low-voltage loads in these exercises; the lessons do not teach mains wiring.

courses.workedExample: A 5 V servo may take 120 mA moving freely but an assumed 700 mA at stall. A 200 mA supply looks adequate in the first condition and fails in the second. lessons.title: Character grids and pixel buffers

lessons.title: Update a useful status screen
lessons.text: Show units, a stable label and a visible fault or stale-data state. Update at a rate useful to the reader instead of clearing and rewriting continuously. courses.summary: Choose a radio path and distinguish hardware connectivity from application messaging.

lessons.title: Choose the communication pattern
lessons.text: WiFi connects an IP-capable node through an access point. Bluetooth LE is useful for nearby device interaction; GATT organises data in services and characteristics. LoRa is a radio modulation used by LoRaWAN, whose network includes gateways and a network server. Choose based on message size, latency, power and infrastructure rather than a promised range alone.

lessons.title: Treat the module as hardware
lessons.text: A separate radio module may connect by UART or SPI and still needs compatible logic, a stable supply and the specified antenna arrangement. Transmit bursts can dominate peak current. Metal enclosures, obstacles and antenna placement affect real links. The virtual ESP32 network models requests and messages, not RF propagation; BLE and LoRa radios are conceptual course topics.

lessons.title: A link is not the whole application
lessons.text: HTTP is a request/response pattern; MQTT publishes messages through a broker to subscribed topics. Neither successful WiFi association nor a sent packet proves that an actuator performed an action. Define payload units, validity, acknowledgements, timeouts and reconnect behaviour. Real deployments need appropriate authentication and transport protection; virtual tutorial credentials are examples only.

courses.workedExample: A room sensor sends a small reading every minute. WiFi with MQTT is convenient where an access point and broker exist. A phone setup interface may suit BLE. courses.summary: Select a power path and review a complete connected-device bill of materials.

lessons.title: Regulators solve different problems
lessons.text: An LDO linear regulator reduces voltage with loss approximately (Vin − Vout) × Iout, plus its own consumption. A buck converter steps down; a boost converter steps up. Check input range, dropout or conversion limits, current rating, efficiency, thermal behaviour and required capacitors. A regulator’s headline current alone is not a full design.

lessons.title: Battery management is a separate function
lessons.text: A battery’s voltage changes with chemistry, state of charge and load. A charger must match the chemistry and cell count; a regulator is not automatically a charger. Protection, cutoff and power-path management are separate requirements. Use a suitable documented battery module and follow its instructions. These courses cover selection and calculations, not building or improvising battery chargers.

lessons.title: Close the parts and validation loop
lessons.text: A complete BOM includes controller, sensors, outputs, interface parts, power conversion, connectors and supporting passives. For each part record voltage, peak and average current, interface and a compatibility check. Validate boot, maximum load, low supply, sensor loss and reconnect behaviour. Add procurement part numbers only after reviewing actual datasheets and module schematics.

courses.workedExample: An LDO supplies 3.3 V at 0.2 A from 5 V. Approximate loss is (5 − 3.3) × 0.2 = 0.34 W, excluding quiescent loss. Output power is 0.66 W, so idealised efficiency is 66%. A switching regulator may reduce loss, but its own efficiency, noise and low-load consumption must be checked for this operating point.

lessons.title: The four jobs of an IoT node
lessons.text: A sensor turns a physical quantity into a signal; a controller reads that signal and decides what to do; an actuator changes an output; a communication interface exchanges information. Arduino Uno/Nano can practise the sensing and control loop without a network. A connected build adds suitable networking hardware or uses a board such as ESP32.

lessons.title: Make a local decision before adding the network
lessons.text: In an Arduino-style sketch, setup runs once after reset and loop repeats. Configure input and output pins, read the input, validate or scale it, then update the output. lessons.title: Send meaningful data and confirm commands
lessons.text: Telemetry is a report from the device, such as an ADC count, temperature with units or an output state. A command requests a change. Keep these meanings separate and document message fields. A network connection does not prove a command ran. Read back the resulting state and define what happens when a request or sensor times out.

lessons.title: Follow power, commands and thrust
lessons.text: A quad-X combines a frame, four motors and props, ESC channels, a battery, a flight controller and sensors. Battery power reaches the motors through ESCs; controller signals command the ESCs. A regulated branch powers the controller. Match each motor and prop direction, confirm connector types and inspect the assembly before interpreting a thrust estimate.

The IMU provides angular-rate and acceleration-related information; the barometer provides pressure-related height information. In the prepared bench lessons, props are removed and the stand is clamped. Confirm sensor response and the intended motor channel at low command before progressing to virtual flight.

courses.title: C, C++ and your first Arduino sketch
courses.summary: Understand the languages and tools, trace setup and loop, and run a complete program on Arduino or ESP32.

lessons.title: Choose a language and a framework
lessons.text: C provides variables, expressions, functions and explicit memory operations. C++ shares much of that syntax and adds facilities such as classes and references; the languages are related but are not identical. Arduino sketches are C++ programs using the Arduino framework. ESP32 is a chip family, not a language: it can use Arduino C++ or Espressif’s ESP-IDF with C and C++. This path teaches their common foundations and the Arduino APIs available in VoltQuest.

lessons.title: Read the sketch lifecycle
lessons.text: A declaration introduces a name and type. A statement performs work and usually ends with a semicolon; braces group a function body or block. Comments explain intent and do not execute. The Arduino framework calls setup once after startup or reset, then calls loop repeatedly. Put one-time configuration in setup and recurring work in loop. A hosted C program commonly starts in main; an ESP-IDF application uses app_main. Those entry points do not replace setup and loop in this simulator.

lessons.title: Build, run, observe and change one thing
lessons.text: For hardware, select the exact board and core, compile the sketch, upload it, then match the serial monitor baud rate to Serial.begin. Arduino’s build process prepares .ino files as C++, finds libraries and links board-specific code. VoltQuest instead interprets a teaching subset locally when you press Run. A successful run here does not validate every compiler feature or hardware library. First predict the output, run it, change one value and compare the observation with your prediction.

courses.workedExample: With a global counter initially zero, setup prints Boot once. The first loop increments the counter to one and prints Tick: 1; after the 500 ms delay the next loop prints Tick: 2. Resetting and running again restarts both the counter and setup. courses.title: C variables, types and arithmetic
courses.summary: Choose numeric types, understand division and conversions, and avoid overflow when moving between AVR and ESP32.

lessons.title: Name values and give them a type
lessons.text: Initialize every variable before reading it. Use const for a setting that should not change, bool for a true/false decision, an integer for counts, and float for fractional measurements. Names are case-sensitive and should carry meaning or units, such as temperatureC. In these Uno/Nano profiles int is 16 bits; on ESP32/S3 it is 32 bits. uint8_t stores 0 through 255, and unsigned long is 32 bits on these boards. These sizes are board facts, not a universal promise about C.

lessons.title: Evaluate expressions before storing them
lessons.text: Operators combine values before assignment. Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition; parentheses make intent clear. For positive integers, 17 / 5 produces 3 and 17 % 5 produces remainder 2. Using 5.0 makes the division floating-point, giving 3.4. Storing 17 / 5 in a float still stores 3.0 because integer division already happened. Cast or widen an operand before the calculation, and never use a zero divisor.

lessons.title: Prevent overflow and separate model behavior
lessons.text: A wider destination cannot repair an overflow that occurred in a narrower expression. On AVR, use 1000L * 1000 for a million: the L makes an operand long before multiplication. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range, which is useful for clocks. Signed overflow is undefined in native C/C++; do not rely on it. VoltQuest deliberately wraps signed arithmetic as a teaching approximation. Check bounds before arithmetic and narrowing conversions, and use compiler warnings when testing on actual hardware.

courses.workedExample: Suppose 17 samples share five time slots. Integer division assigns three samples per slot and the remainder is two. A fractional average requires 17 / 5.0, which Serial.println prints as 3.40 by default. For a million-microsecond calculation on Uno, 1000L * 1000 evaluates as long. Merely assigning 1000 * 1000 to a long is not a portable fix for signed int overflow.

courses.summary: Turn sensor values into explicit decisions and understand active-low buttons, comparisons and branch boundaries.

lessons.title: Write mutually exclusive decisions
lessons.text: An if statement runs its block when a condition is true. An else if chain tests later conditions only when earlier ones were false; else covers the remaining case. Use == for comparison and = for assignment. Decide whether a threshold includes its boundary: temperatureC >= 30 includes exactly 30, while > 30 does not. Always test below, at and above each threshold, and initialize the output so that every path has a defined result.

lessons.title: Combine conditions with Boolean logic
lessons.text: Logical AND (&&) requires both conditions; OR (||) needs at least one; ! negates a condition. C and C++ short-circuit these operators: in valid && reading > limit, the right side is not evaluated when valid is false. Parentheses help show the intended grouping. Bitwise & and | operate on integer bits and are different operators. A sensor validity flag should be checked before using its measurement to command an output.

lessons.title: Interpret inputs before controlling outputs
lessons.text: pinMode configures a pin; digitalRead returns its logical level and digitalWrite commands an output level. With INPUT_PULLUP and a button to ground, released reads HIGH and pressed reads LOW. Convert this electrical convention into a clear Boolean such as pressed = digitalRead(buttonPin) == LOW. Reading HIGH does not mean a button is universally pressed. Floating inputs have no reliable default, and ESP32 GPIO must not receive a 5 V signal.

courses.workedExample: For valid = true, enabled = true and temperatureC = 30, the expression valid && enabled && temperatureC >= 30 is true. At 29 it is false. Setting valid to false disables cooling even at 40. A separate button exercise uses INPUT_PULLUP: pressing connects the input to ground, so the software turns LOW into pressed = true before deciding the LED state.

courses.title: Loops, functions and variable scope
courses.summary: Break a program into bounded loops and reusable functions with clear inputs, results and lifetimes.

lessons.title: Make iteration finite and intentional
lessons.text: A for loop puts initialization, continuation condition and update together. for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) visits 0, 1 and 2. A while loop checks before each iteration; do/while checks after the body and runs at least once. break exits the nearest loop, while continue skips to its next iteration. Check that some action can make the continuation condition false. Long loops delay other work in a cooperative firmware program.

lessons.title: Give a function one clear job
lessons.text: A function has a return type, name, parameters and body. Parameters describe its inputs; return sends a result to the caller. void means there is no returned value. Passing an ordinary int parameter copies its value, so changing that parameter does not change the caller’s variable. Prefer functions whose result depends on explicit inputs, such as clamping a requested percentage. A declaration or prototype states the signature; native C/C++ needs a declaration before a call.

lessons.title: Separate scope from lifetime
lessons.text: Scope determines where a name can be used; lifetime determines how long its object exists. An ordinary local is created for a call or block. A global remains across loop calls. A static local also retains its value across calls while its name stays local. Avoid shadowing a global with an identically named local, because updates may affect the wrong variable. Recursion needs a terminating case and consumes stack on hardware; bounded iteration is often easier to budget on small boards.

courses.workedExample: clampPercent(-20) returns 0, clampPercent(50) returns 50, and clampPercent(120) returns 100. The function returns a decision without printing or changing global state, making these three cases easy to test. A loop can call it for several requests. If a local parameter named value changes inside clampPercent, the original integer in the caller remains unchanged unless the caller assigns the returned result.

courses.title: Arrays, C strings, memory and bit flags
courses.summary: Store samples and text with explicit bounds, reason about pointers, and encode small sets of Boolean flags.

lessons.title: Store and traverse fixed-size arrays
lessons.text: An array groups elements of one type in consecutive storage. int samples[3] has valid indices 0, 1 and 2; index 3 is outside the array. Initialize elements and carry the element count alongside data. In a scope where the object is an actual array, sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]) gives its length. It does not recover an array length from a pointer parameter. Use a sufficiently wide accumulator before summing many sensor readings.

lessons.title: Bound C strings and understand pointer lifetime
lessons.text: A C string is a char array terminated by a zero byte, written as backslash-zero in source. A buffer of eight bytes holds at most seven text characters plus that terminator. An array commonly converts to a pointer to its first element when passed to a function. A pointer refers to storage; it does not own a length or extend that storage’s lifetime. Never return a pointer to an ordinary local array. General pointer arithmetic and native memory access are outside VoltQuest’s teaching subset.

lessons.title: Represent independent flags with bits
lessons.text: Bitwise operations work on integer bit patterns. A mask 1U << 2 selects bit two, whose numeric value is four. flags | mask sets that bit, flags & mask tests it, and flags & ~mask clears it when stored back into the flag type. Use unsigned operands, valid shift counts and parentheses. Logical && combines truth values instead. A fixed buffer and a byte of flags have predictable storage, unlike repeatedly growing dynamic text on a small microcontroller.

courses.workedExample: For samples 100, 200 and 300, a long accumulator totals 600; dividing by 3.0 produces 200.00. The array length is three, although its byte size differs between Uno and ESP32 because int differs. Starting flags at zero, setting bit two yields 4 and testing that mask yields true. Clearing the same mask returns flags to zero. None of these operations require reading outside the sample array.

courses.summary: Read constructors and method calls, distinguish String from C strings, and understand the limits of the browser subset.

lessons.title: Read object and library APIs
lessons.text: A C++ class describes a type; an object is an instance with its own state. A constructor initializes it, and a method operates through that object, as in servo.write(90). Include the library header before declaring its types, and call begin or attach when the API requires initialization. Different objects can hold different state. VoltQuest provides selected native library classes such as Servo and WebServer; arbitrary user-defined classes, inheritance and the complete C++ standard library are not implemented.

lessons.title: Distinguish values, references and managed text
lessons.text: Arduino String is a C++ text object, different from a zero-terminated char buffer. String methods such as trim and toUpperCase modify that object; length returns its current character count. On hardware, growth can allocate memory, so keep incoming messages bounded. A C++ reference is an alias to an existing object rather than an ordinary value copy. General reference parameters and object ownership features require a native toolchain here. Use the documented subset instead of assuming every C++ example can run in the browser.

lessons.title: Organize an embedded program for growth
lessons.text: Use named constants for configuration, small functions for calculations, and enums for a fixed set of states. A struct groups related fields such as a value and its validity flag. In a native project, headers declare interfaces and .cpp files implement them; Arduino preprocesses .ino files but does not automatically include every header. Advanced C++ adds templates and resource lifetime techniques such as RAII. Study those with a compiler and tests after this path; the simulator is not a full C++ or ESP-IDF environment.

courses.workedExample: Start with String command = " on ". Its length is four because both spaces count. trim removes the surrounding spaces, toUpperCase changes on to ON, and equals("ON") returns true. The program prints 4, ON, then 1. This illustrates an object’s changing state and method calls; it does not imply a char array automatically has those methods or that unbounded String growth is safe on a small board.

courses.title: Arduino and ESP32: ADC, PWM and portability
courses.summary: Connect numeric code to real inputs and outputs while accounting for pin maps, resolution and voltage differences.

lessons.title: Convert an ADC count deliberately
lessons.text: analogRead returns a count, not a voltage. The Uno/Nano learning profiles use 10-bit counts from 0 to 1023; ESP32/S3 default to 12 bits from 0 to 4095. Normalize by the chosen full-scale count before comparing percentages or converting units. Use floating-point division or widened integer arithmetic. VoltQuest models an ideal linear ADC; real ESP32 attenuation, calibration and usable voltage range depend on the chip. More bits do not automatically mean more measurement accuracy.

lessons.title: Distinguish PWM from an analog voltage source
lessons.text: PWM switches a digital output between LOW and HIGH. Duty cycle describes the fraction of each period spent HIGH; frequency describes periods per second. analogWrite commonly accepts 0–255 on Uno PWM pins. ESP32 LEDC provides configurable resolution and frequency. Current Arduino-ESP32 APIs use pin-based ledcAttach and ledcWrite; the existing VoltQuest PWM tutorial uses the older channel-based teaching adapter. Check the installed core’s API before transferring code. PWM does not make a GPIO a calibrated DAC.

lessons.title: Port the circuit as well as the code
lessons.text: A board change can alter supply voltage, ADC pin, PWM capability and integer width. The prepared potentiometer labs use A0 on AVR, GPIO34 on classic ESP32 and GPIO4 on S3. Classic ESP32 GPIO34 is input-only and belongs to ADC1, useful while Wi-Fi operates; do not generalize its pin map to S3. Use the prepared board variant and common ground, protect 3.3 V inputs, and keep conversion constants next to the board-specific pin configuration.

courses.workedExample: An illustrative ADC count of 512 on a 10-bit scale represents 512 / 1023.0, about 0.5005 of full scale. Multiplying by 100 gives 50.05%. Integer mapping 512L * 255 / 1023 produces duty 127 because it truncates. This is an intentional rounding policy, not a faulty sensor. On ESP32, use a 4095 maximum and its actual ADC pin; do not reuse the AVR denominator blindly.

courses.title: Responsive timing, debounce and rollover
courses.summary: Schedule work with millis, reason about unsigned clocks, and distinguish a button edge from contact bounce.

lessons.title: Poll deadlines without blocking the whole loop
lessons.text: delay pauses the current sketch path, so that path cannot poll a button or service a server while waiting. Store a previous timestamp and compare elapsed time against an interval in each loop call. Keep separate timestamps for independent jobs such as blinking and telemetry. Assigning previous = now skips missed periods; adding interval to previous preserves the nominal schedule but needs a bounded catch-up policy. Return to loop quickly enough for every job’s required responsiveness.

lessons.title: Use unsigned elapsed-time subtraction
lessons.text: On these boards millis uses a 32-bit unsigned long millisecond clock. Compute unsigned long elapsed = now - previous, then compare elapsed >= interval. Modular subtraction works through one wrap when the actual elapsed duration is less than the clock’s full range and checks are frequent enough. Comparing now >= previous + interval can fail when the addition wraps. Use UL constants for time arithmetic, keep intervals small and avoid mixing signed values with the unsigned clock.

lessons.title: Separate raw input, stable input and edges
lessons.text: A mechanical button can bounce between levels during one press. Remember the latest raw reading and when it changed. Accept it as stable only after it remains unchanged for a chosen debounce interval, such as 30 ms in an experiment. Compare the new stable state with the previous stable state to detect one press edge. Counting every loop while held counts many events; edge detection without debounce can still count bounce. The browser button is idealized unless a test injects rapid changes.

courses.workedExample: Imagine a clock previously at 4294967290 ms and now at 5 ms. Unsigned 32-bit subtraction gives 11 ms, so a 10 ms interval has elapsed even though the new timestamp is numerically smaller. Separately, a raw button that changes at 100 ms and remains unchanged becomes stable at 130 ms under a 30 ms policy. A second raw change at 110 ms would restart that waiting interval until 140 ms.

courses.title: Serial protocols and systematic debugging
courses.summary: Parse complete bounded commands, recover from malformed input, and diagnose syntax, runtime and logic failures.

lessons.title: Treat serial input as a stream of bytes
lessons.text: Serial.available reports how many received bytes can be read; Serial.read consumes one byte and can return -1 when none is available. A message can arrive in several fragments or several messages can arrive together. Define a delimiter, such as newline, before interpreting commands. Carriage return and newline are separate characters. This example ignores carriage return and finishes a command at newline. Waiting for one byte is not evidence that the whole message has arrived.

lessons.title: Bound the frame and reject invalid commands
lessons.text: Choose a maximum command length and reject oversized input until the next delimiter. Do not interpret the valid-looking tail of a rejected frame as a new command. Compare complete commands exactly, such as ON and OFF, and keep output unchanged for unknown commands. Numeric parsers also need syntax and range checks; accepting a numeric prefix does not validate the rest of a message. Keep parsing separate from applying a command so malformed input cannot partially update device state.

lessons.title: Debug with predictions and small observations
lessons.text: A syntax error prevents compilation, a runtime error occurs during execution, and a logic error produces the wrong behavior despite running. Start with the first diagnostic and its source line, then reduce the program to the smallest failing case. Log inputs, state transitions and outcomes with units or labels. Match serial baud on hardware and avoid flooding the output: printing consumes time and buffer space. Test partial frames, back-to-back commands, empty input and recovery after overflow, not only the happy path.

courses.workedExample: Receive O first: no command is ready. Receive N followed by newline: accept ON once. Receive ONX followed by newline: reject it without treating its ON prefix as a command. With a maximum of eight characters, nine characters followed by ON and newline must reject the entire frame. A fresh OFF followed by newline should then succeed, proving the parser recovered at the delimiter.
courses.application: Write a command protocol before implementing it: accepted words, case rules, line ending, maximum length and rejection behavior. Build a test table containing fragmented, invalid and oversized input with the expected unchanged or updated state.

lab.task: Run the single-character dispatcher first. Then paste the framed example and send ON; and OFF; using the serial input. The example accepts semicolon as well as newline, so a single-line input can send complete frames.

The byte is a valid command

options.text: Yes, use the last two bytes
Only if the LED is off

questions.prompt: Why wait for a delimiter before applying a framed command?

options.text: The message may still be incomplete
Every Serial.read returns a full line

questions.explanation: Serial is a byte stream; the protocol must define when a message is complete.

questions.prompt: The only accepted commands are ON and OFF. What should ONX do?
questions.explanation: Exact matching rejects malformed extensions rather than accepting a prefix.

questions.prompt: A program compiles and runs but prints the wrong average. Which failure is this?
questions.explanation: Successful execution does not prove the calculation or behavior is correct.

questions.prompt: What is the best first response to several compiler diagnostics?

options.text: Inspect the first relevant diagnostic and source line
Increase the serial baud until they disappear

questions.explanation: One early syntax mistake can cause many later diagnostic messages.

questions.prompt: Why can excessive Serial printing change timing?

options.text: Transmission uses time and finite buffering

questions.explanation: When output buffers fill, printing may wait for transmission capacity.

formulas.title: Estimate serial transmission time
formulas.symbols: baud is bits per second; 8N1 uses approximately ten transmitted bits per character.
formulas.assumptions: An 8N1 serial link without additional protocol overhead; buffering can defer when waiting becomes visible.
formulas.example: 96 characters at 9600 baud occupy about 100 ms of wire time.

courses.title: State machines and a local controller capstone
courses.summary: Combine functions, timing and explicit state into a controller whose transitions can be tested and explained.

lessons.title: Describe states, events and transitions first
lessons.text: A state machine stores which behavior is active. Define a small set of named states, the events or conditions that leave each state, and the next state. A transition table makes omissions visible before coding. Entry actions happen once when entering a state; ongoing actions happen while it remains active. Store the entry timestamp when a transition occurs rather than resetting it on every loop call, which would prevent a timeout from ever completing.

lessons.title: Use switch and preserve output invariants
lessons.text: switch selects a case from the current state. End a case with break unless fall-through is explicitly intended; default should restore a defined safe state when an unexpected value occurs. Derive outputs from one authoritative state instead of unrelated flags that can contradict each other. For a traffic signal, an invariant could be that conflicting green outputs are never on together. A working sequence is not enough: also test that forbidden combinations never occur between transitions.

lessons.title: Turn requirements into observable tests
lessons.text: Write a timeline of inputs and expected state before pressing Run. Cover startup, each transition, time boundaries, repeated input and return to the initial state. Combine the earlier bounded functions, input validation and separate timers into a local controller. Hysteresis uses different on and off thresholds and remembers its previous output inside the gap. Document which event wins if a sensor fault and a user request occur together, then verify that priority with alternate input sequences.

courses.workedExample: The demonstration cycles STOP for 300 ms, GO for 200 ms and WAIT for 100 ms. A transition helper updates both state and enteredAt, then reports the new name once. At roughly 300, 500 and 600 ms the output reports GO, WAIT and STOP. These are serial state labels, not a safety-rated traffic controller. The linked LED state-machine lab lets you relate an actual output pattern to the same state-and-time reasoning.
courses.application: Build a local alarm design with idle, warning and fault states. Specify entry conditions, output behavior and recovery for each, then add an event table and test a sensor fault during an active warning before taking the exam.

lab.task: Trace the prepared four-state LED beacon. Change one duration and check the complete cycle as well as every transition.

extraLabs.task: Move the pot up and down through both thresholds. Explain why the same middle reading can legitimately preserve either previous output state.

practice.prompt: When should a state entry timestamp be updated?

options.text: When the transition enters that state

practice.explanation: The elapsed time must measure duration in the state, not duration since the last loop.

practice.prompt: What does an unintended missing break in switch risk?

options.text: A compile error in every case

practice.explanation: C/C++ switch permits fall-through, so break expresses the intended exit.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a transition table?

options.text: Current state, event and next state

questions.explanation: A transition describes how an event changes a specific current state.

questions.prompt: What is a useful invariant for conflicting green signals?

options.text: They must never be on together
Their names must have equal length

questions.explanation: The invariant forbids an unsafe output combination throughout the sequence.

questions.prompt: A hysteresis controller is between its on and off thresholds. What determines its output?
questions.explanation: Hysteresis intentionally remembers state inside the threshold gap.

questions.prompt: What should a state machine do with an unexpected state value?

options.text: Use a defined recovery or safe default

questions.explanation: A default case makes recovery explicit and keeps outputs defined.

questions.prompt: Why test a fault and user request arriving together?

options.text: To verify the specified event priority
To make the timer run backwards

questions.explanation: Conflicting events expose whether the implementation follows the intended priority.

formulas.title: State duration and cycle length
formulas.symbols: Each term is a state duration in milliseconds.
formulas.assumptions: The sequence has three timed states; small loop and reporting overhead adds timing tolerance.
formulas.example: 300 + 200 + 100 = 600 ms nominally, so the state sequence repeats about every 0.6 s.

courses.title: ESP32 C++: Wi-Fi and HTTP device control
courses.summary: Use library objects and callbacks to expose explicit commands and observable status on a virtual ESP32.

lessons.title: Choose Arduino-ESP32 or native ESP-IDF deliberately
lessons.text: Arduino-ESP32 provides setup, loop and familiar Arduino APIs on supported ESP chips. ESP-IDF is Espressif’s native development framework with its own build system, app_main entry point and C/C++ APIs. Native projects can use tasks and synchronization, but VoltQuest does not simulate FreeRTOS or arbitrary ESP-IDF programs. GPIO maps differ across ESP32 and S3, while both use 3.3 V logic here. Keep long-term library instances alive and configure pins before handling commands.

lessons.title: Separate connection state from application readiness
lessons.text: Station mode connects to an access point; softAP makes the device an access point. An IP address or connected flag does not prove that a server route is registered or being serviced. In VoltQuest, softAP and the named VoltNet network are virtual and never contact your router. A native deployment needs its own network configuration and failure policy. Avoid unbounded connection waits in a responsive device; periodic retry and a defined disconnected state belong in a complete hardware design.

lessons.title: Register handlers and report actual state
lessons.text: A callback is a function passed for later invocation. server.on registers a route handler, begin starts the server, and handleClient services pending requests from loop. Give commands explicit meanings: ON sets on, OFF sets off, and status reports the current state. Repeating ON should leave the device on instead of toggling it. Check HTTP status and observed output together. These virtual GET commands are learning conveniences; a deployed device needs an appropriate authenticated command interface and network design.

courses.workedExample: The sample registers /on, /off and /status for GPIO18. Requesting /on sets the stored state and pin HIGH and returns ON. Repeating /on has the same result. /status returns the stored state without changing it; /off sets both state and pin LOW. An unknown route returns 404 through the teaching server. If handleClient is omitted, being an access point still does not process those requests.
courses.application: Use the prepared ESP32 LED circuit to implement explicit ON, OFF and status routes. Test startup OFF, repeated ON, status without mutation, OFF and an unknown path. Record the HTTP response beside the observed LED state.

lab.task: Run the command/status lab on ESP32 and S3. Request /on and /status, inspect the LED, then repeat /on to check that setting a state is different from toggling.

practice.prompt: Which framework uses app_main rather than the Arduino sketch entry points?
practice.explanation: ESP-IDF has its own application entry and build environment.

practice.prompt: Which call services pending requests in this WebServer loop?
practice.explanation: Registration and begin are initialization; handleClient performs ongoing request service.

questions.explanation: Soft access point mode lets the device act as an access point; this simulator models it virtually.

questions.prompt: Why is an IP address alone insufficient evidence that /on works?

options.text: The route must be registered and requests serviced

questions.explanation: Connection state and application readiness are separate conditions.

questions.prompt: What should two identical explicit ON commands do?
questions.explanation: An explicit state-setting command is repeatable without reversing the result.

questions.prompt: What is a callback?

options.text: A function supplied for later invocation
A variable that always starts at 80

questions.explanation: A server invokes the registered function when the matching request is serviced.

options.text: Yes, all native APIs are implemented
Only by changing the file extension
No, it uses the supported Arduino teaching subset

courses.title: MQTT and the connected-controller capstone
courses.summary: Combine bounded callbacks, explicit commands, telemetry and command expiry in an ESP32 program you can test.

lessons.title: Separate transport, topic and payload
lessons.text: MQTT clients communicate through a broker. A subscription selects topics; a publish sends a payload on a topic. Connecting is not the same as subscribing, and publishing a command is not proof that a device applied it. PubSubClient uses a transport object, a broker configuration and regular loop service. Its callback receives a topic, payload bytes and explicit length. Do not assume payload bytes are zero-terminated text. The VoltQuest broker and Wi-Fi are virtual, with simplified connectivity rather than real cloud networking.

lessons.title: Validate a command and give it an expiry policy
lessons.text: Check the exact topic, allowed length and complete command before changing state. Keep invalid messages from renewing a command lease. An ON command may grant a short interval of activity, after which the device returns to OFF unless a fresh valid command renews it. Store the acceptance timestamp and use unsigned elapsed subtraction. OFF should apply immediately. A lease bounds stale intent, but it is not authentication and does not replace hardware interlocks or an explicit disconnect policy in a deployed device.

lessons.title: Verify the complete connected control loop
lessons.text: A useful capstone has one authoritative output state, separate network and timer service, and telemetry that agrees with the applied state. Test a valid command, repeated renewal, malformed payload, wrong topic, explicit OFF and lease expiry. The sample also accepts serial characters 1 and 0 as local test inputs so the prepared LED lab can demonstrate the same command handler. Boot connection waits are bounded here; production reconnect, delivery acknowledgement, authentication and real radio behavior require a hardware implementation beyond this teaching example.

courses.workedExample: After the virtual connection is ready, sending serial 1 applies ON, lights GPIO18 and publishes ON on course/state. With no renewal, a two-second lease expires, the LED switches OFF and OFF is published. Send 1 again before expiry to restart the lease. A wrong MQTT topic or malformed payload must neither turn the LED on nor extend its lifetime. Serial 0 exercises immediate OFF through the same application function.
courses.application: Use the LED lab for local command and expiry tests, then study MQTT publication in the sensor lab. For a full sandbox experiment, build the same GPIO18 LED circuit and use the IoT inspector to inject ON or OFF on course/cmd. Compare telemetry with the actual output and test invalid input during an active lease.

lab.task: Run the prepared sensor publisher on ESP32/S3. Change temperature and inspect the published payload, then identify the transport object, topic and client.loop call.

extraLabs.task: Choose ESP32 or ESP32-S3 and paste the capstone sketch. Send 1 to light the prepared GPIO18 LED, renew with another 1, then observe automatic OFF after two seconds without renewal.

No, only an accepted command may renew it
Only if the payload is very long

questions.explanation: Topics connect publishers and subscribers through the broker.

options.text: Matching observed output and reported state

questions.explanation: End-to-end verification checks what the device actually did and reported.

questions.explanation: Topic validation is part of command acceptance, even when payload text looks valid.

questions.prompt: Does a command lease authenticate the sender?

options.text: No, it only limits how long accepted intent remains active
Yes, if the LED is bright

questions.explanation: Authentication, transport security and hardware protection are separate deployment concerns.
